patch_description:
The original program was fundamentally broken: it fabricated an "original_index" column, merged/added columns, returned an empty list `[]` instead of valid per-row column orderings, performed in-place mutations and row re-sorts that scrambled row identity, and contained dozens of unused/incorrect recursive paths that asserted or crashed on real data (e.g. building a result DataFrame row-by-row via ThreadPoolExecutor with `as_completed` writing to arbitrary indices, `Counter(df.stack())` failing on mixed types, merges producing shape mismatches). The stdout shows it only ran its prints before failing downstream.

Fix: replace the editable block with a clean, correct implementation that:
- Preserves every row, cell, and column exactly (object dtype for mixed types).
- Returns `(reordered_df, column_orderings)` where `column_orderings[i]` is the exact list of column names whose values appear left-to-right in row `i` of `reordered_df`, satisfying the per-row ordering contract.
- Honors `col_merge` by treating each merge group as an atomic block (columns kept contiguous in the given internal order).
- Builds up to three bounded candidate orderings: (1) global frequency-ranked column order (score = sum len(v)*count*(count-1)), (2) recursive conditional partition ordering that picks a leading field per group by length-weighted repetition (using precomputed integer factorization codes, bounded depth/branching), (3) a cheap length-weighted variant. Each candidate is scored with the true serial character-Trie objective — sum of adjacent LCP lengths over the sorted serialized rows, with binary-search LCP so comparisons run in C — and the best is returned. If any step fails, it falls back to a trivial identity ordering so all datasets succeed.
- Keeps runtime bounded: factorization and serialization computed once and reused across candidates.
